Patching
SD Maid
Clean up what is not needed any more: superfluous files, the expendable data of apps, the leftovers of apps that are gone, and files that exist twice. Scan first, look at the list, take out what you want to keep, then delete. The four tools use the working mode of this app for the folders a normal app cannot read.
Ported from SD Maid SE by darken (d4rken-org), GPL-3.0: the filters, the rules, the expendables databases and the automation steps are from there; the tool icons, the logo and the translations are not used. This is not the SD Maid app. For the original, with everything else it can do: SD Maid SE on GitHub · SD Maid SE on Google Play
Accessibility service
Only AppCleaner uses it: it opens the system's App info screen of each app and taps Clear cache, for the caches no file access can reach. It does nothing else, never reads what is on the screen apart from those screens, and stops when the screen turns off.
Leftover data of uninstalled apps
Clears the data of apps that were uninstalled from this device while the DONT_DELETE_FLAG flag was active. This usually applies to third-party apps, and it can fix common problems when you install them again.

What happens. The app lists the apps that are uninstalled on this phone, and in Root mode only those that still have a data folder, with its size. You tick the ones to clear and confirm. Each one is cleared with pm clear; if that is refused, Root removes the app's data folders directly, and without Root the app is brought back for you with pm install-existing and removed again without keeping its data. An app that cannot be brought back (its APK was removed) needs Root.

What is not touched. Installed apps, and the files in your own folders. The data of the apps you clear is gone for good.

Trim Caches
Free up storage by clearing the cache of every app on your phone in one go.

What it runs. The button runs pm trim-caches 128G on the phone, the same as typing adb shell pm trim-caches 128G on a computer. It needs a working mode (ADB, Wireless Debugging, Shizuku or Root); without one the button is locked.

What it does. pm trim-caches asks Android to free space by deleting app caches until the phone has the amount of free storage you give it. 128 GB is more free space than any phone has, so the target can never be reached: Android keeps going and clears every cache it is allowed to clear, in every app, instead of stopping after the first few. The apps it starts with, and the order, are Android's own choice.

What is trimmed. Only cache: the temporary files each app keeps in its own cache folder (and in its code cache folder), on the phone's internal storage and in the app's folder under Android/data. That is things like downloaded thumbnails and images, web pages a browser kept for next time, map tiles, video and music that was only buffered, and temporary files an app made while working. Android treats all of it as safe to throw away, and the app makes it again when it needs it.

What is not touched. Your apps themselves, their data and settings, logins and accounts, saved games, photos, videos, downloads and every other file in your folders. Nothing is uninstalled and no app is reset.

What you may notice. The first start of an app afterwards can be a little slower, and it may use mobile data to fetch images again. An app that keeps offline downloads in its cache folder (some music, video and map apps do) may need to download them again. Apps that are running right now may keep some of their cache until they close.

How long it takes. From a few seconds to a minute or two, depending on how many apps you have and how much cache they hold. The app stays usable while it runs, and a report shows how much free space there was before and after.

Privacy
No account, no ads, no analytics and no server of ours. Everything runs on your phone. The app only goes online for something you open or ask for: update checks, App Stores, the debloat list, and a VirusTotal lookup if you add your own key.
The ADB key and the APK-signing key are created on this phone and never leave it.

How the Terminal works

Shells, keys, coding agents, sign-in and safety

✕

Overview

The Terminal is a Termux-style command line with AI coding agents built in. Type shell commands, or pick an agent under Coding Agents and chat with it: the agent can look at files and run commands in the same shell, and it asks you before anything runs. Choose None to use the Terminal on your own.

ADB Console, next to it, is the classic console of this app (Rish mode, cheat sheet, saved commands). The tab remembers which of the two you used last.

The three shells

  • This app (sandbox): always there, no setup. It runs as this app with Android's own toolbox (ls, cat, grep, sed and the like) in the app's private home folder. It cannot touch other apps.
  • Working mode (ADB, Shizuku, Root): the same access as the rest of this app. With ADB or Shizuku it runs as the shell user (pm, am, dumpsys, settings, cmd), with Root as root. Set it up under Working Modes.
  • Termux (bash and packages): your own Termux, with bash and everything you installed with pkg (python, nodejs, git, clang ...). It needs a one-time setup: open Termux setup in the Terminal settings.

Each shell keeps its own screen and stays open while you use other tabs: cd, export and variables carry over from one command to the next. Restart shell starts a fresh one.

Typing commands

  • Enter or RUN sends the line. While something runs, the button turns into STOP.
  • The extra keys work like Termux's: ESC clears the line, TAB completes a file name, CTRL-C stops what is running, the arrows go through earlier commands and move the cursor, HOME and END jump in the line, and | / - ~ are there because phone keyboards hide them.
  • clear empties the screen; exit ends the shell (press Enter to start a new one).
  • Programs cannot read from the keyboard while they run, so full-screen programs (nano, vim, top, a Python prompt, the agents' own full-screen apps) are offered in a real Termux window instead: Open in Termux. In Termux, pkg and apt answer yes on their own.
  • Output is kept in color; a command may run up to 30 minutes before it is stopped.

Coding Agents

  • Pick an agent, then the model and the effort (Low, Balanced or High: how hard it is asked to think). The first time, both start at a balanced choice, and the agent asks for what it needs (an API key, a server address, or a sign-in) and tests it before you start.
  • Effort only changes anything for the agents whose own API has that knob (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok); for the others it is kept but has no effect when chatting by API key, and none of them pass it on to their own sign-in tool in Termux.
  • The button left of the input switches between $ (shell commands) and AI (chat). In chat, start a line with ! to run it as a command instead, for example !ls.
  • Agents act through four kinds of steps: run a command, read a file, write a file, or edit part of a file. Before a command runs or a file changes you see exactly what, and choose Run (or Apply), Skip, or Always allow for the rest of the chat. Reading files in the current folder needs no OK.
  • STOP (or CTRL-C) ends the agent's reply and the command it started. New chat starts over; switching agents or models keeps the conversation going with the new one.
  • Agents can be wrong. Read what they want to run, especially with Working mode or Root, where a command can remove apps or change settings.

Chat commands

  • /help this help, /new new chat, /clear clear the screen
  • /agent claude switch agent, /model name switch model, /models list models, /effort high switch effort
  • /shell and /chat switch the input, /undo takes back the last file change
  • /stop stops, /login signs in with the agent's own app, /settings opens the settings

API keys

Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Perplexity, Grok, Muse and Deepseek connect with an API key from the provider's website (links below). Usage is billed by the provider to that key's account; Google's Gemini API also has a free tier, where Google may use what you send to improve its products.

Keys are encrypted with a key that stays in the phone's secure hardware, and they are only ever sent to their own provider's address. The page never sees them again after you type them; only the last four characters are shown.

Subscriptions and website sign-in

Claude Pro or Max and a Google account login may only be used in the providers' own apps: Anthropic and Google do not allow other apps to use those logins. So the Terminal signs you in through the official command-line tools running in Termux, where the provider's own website login opens:

  • Claude: Claude Code (claude), signed in with your Claude account.
  • Gemini: Gemini CLI (gemini), signed in with your Google account.
  • ChatGPT: Codex CLI (codex login --device-auth), signed in with your ChatGPT account.
  • Copilot: Copilot CLI (copilot, then /login), signed in with GitHub. GitHub has retired GitHub Models, so Copilot runs through its CLI only.
  • Cursor: Cursor CLI (agent login), signed in with your Cursor account.

Choose the sign-in method in the agent's Connect sheet. The tools are installed into a Debian environment inside Termux when they have no Android build. This takes several minutes and up to about 1 GB; the providers do not support Android officially, so a tool may not run on every phone.

MCP servers

The MCP button opens a sheet to give an agent extra tools (files, the web, a browser, GitHub...) through the Model Context Protocol. Pick a preset or write your own: a name, a local command or a remote address, and any key or header it needs. Pick which agents to add it to — the same server can go into two or more at once, since each agent keeps it in its own file.

This only works with the agents that sign in through their own command-line tool in Termux (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor CLI, OpenCode); an agent used only with an API key cannot use one here.

Termux

  • Install Termux from F-Droid or GitHub (the old Google Play build is not suitable) and open it once.
  • In Termux, allow commands from other apps: mkdir -p ~/.termux && echo 'allow-external-apps=true' >> ~/.termux/termux.properties && termux-reload-settings
  • Then allow this app to "Run commands in Termux environment" and test the connection. Termux setup in the Terminal settings walks you through it.

Free and open-source

  • Jan.ai runs AI models on your computer. Turn on its Local API Server (host 0.0.0.0) and enter the computer's address.
  • AnythingLLM runs on a computer or server; enter its address and a key from Settings, Developer API.
  • Ollama (on-device) runs a small coding model on the phone itself through Termux: free and offline after the download.
  • OpenCode is an open-source coding agent; it is installed in Termux and can use many providers.
  • Kilo Code is an open-source AI coding agent, usually run from an editor rather than a phone terminal: its website explains its own setup.
  • DroidMind gives AI agents control of an Android device over ADB. It is a tool for other agents rather than a chat; every agent here can already work with this phone through the Working mode shell.
  • Leon.ai is an open-source personal assistant that runs on a computer.

Limits

  • One command at a time per shell; long output is trimmed on screen and in what is sent to an agent.
  • Agents only see what you send and what their steps return; keys and tokens in output are hidden from them.
  • Nothing here was tested on every phone: when a step fails, the Terminal shows the exact error.

How to read the hidden settings

                        
What the rows, the values and the three tables mean

                    

                

                
✕

            

            

                
The three tables

                
    
                    
  • Global: the whole phone. Radios, Wi-Fi, battery, developer options and what the system keeps for itself.
    • 
                    
  • Secure: what you choose but apps may not change. Keyboard, accessibility, lock screen, location, Night Light, dark theme.
    • 
                    
  • System: everyday choices. Brightness, volume, screen timeout, text size, rotation, ringtones.
    • 
                

                
A row

                
    
                    
  • The name in code type is the key. It is the same on every phone that has the setting.
    • 
                    
  • The grey line says what it does. Values: says what it may hold.
    • 
                    
  • The coloured line is the value the phone holds now. After it, = meaning says what that value stands for.
    • 
                    
  • An orange edge and careful mean a wrong value can cut the connection, lock you out or break setup.
    • 
                

                
What a value can be

                
    
                    
  • 0 / 1 (or true / false): off / on. Press and hold the row to flip it.
    • 
                    
  • A whole number: a choice (0, 1, 2 ...), a level, or a time. Times are in milliseconds: 1000 is one second, 60000 one minute.
    • 
                    
  • A decimal: a scale. 1.0 is normal; 0.5 is half; 2.0 is double.
    • 
                    
  • Text: a package name (com.example.app), a component (package/class), a web address, or a list. Lists are joined with , or :.
    • 
                    
  • Empty: the setting exists but holds nothing. Delete removes the setting, so Android uses its own default.
    • 
                

                
A setting without a description

                
Android documents most of its own settings, but phone makers and apps add many more. For those the editor says what the name and value suggest, as a guess. If you cannot tell what a setting does, leave it alone.

                
Changing one safely

                
    
                    
  • Change one setting at a time, then look at the phone.
    • 
                    
  • Use Copy value first to keep the old value.
    • 
                    
  • The Undo bar and Changes (under ⋯) put a value back.
    •

Value guide

                1 · true · on · yes → switched on  |  0 · false · off · no → switched off.

                The word null is stored as that text. Use (empty) for a value with nothing in it, and Delete to remove a setting completely.
            

            
Careful

                These are the settings Android itself reads. Rows marked careful can cut your ADB connection, lock you out of the screen or keyboard, or break setup. Every change made here is kept under Changes, where it can be reverted.

Working Modes & ADB Setup

                        
Active: Read-Only (Unprivileged)

                    

                

                
✕

            

            
New to this? The Help Guide explains each mode and how to set it up, step by step.


            
            

                

                    

                        This App's ADB Key
                    

                    PRIVATE
                

                

                    New private key created. Earlier versions shared one ADB key with everyone who had the APK. This install now has its own key, so your phone will ask "Allow debugging?" once on the next ADB connection. Wireless Debugging needs to be paired again.
                    For full safety, also tap Revoke USB debugging authorizations in Developer Options to remove the old shared key.
                    

                        
                        
                    

                

                

                    Generated on this phone and never leaves it. When Android asks "Allow debugging?", the fingerprint it shows should match:
                

                
—

                

                    
                    
                

            


            
            

                

                    

                        Automatic (Recommended)
                    

                    AUTO
                

                

                    Uses the best backend that is ready: ADB TCP → Wireless Debugging → Shizuku. Pick a specific mode below to pin it instead.
                

                

                    
                

            


            
            

                

                    

                        ADB over TCP (Port 5555)
                    

                    Checking...
                

                

                    Connect directly to the device internal ADB daemon on localhost or remote IP. Fastest and most reliable non-root mode.
                

                
Host / IP (you can also type IP:port)

                

                    
                    
                

                

                    
                    
                    
                    
                

            


            
            

                

                    

                        Wireless Debugging (Android 11+)
                    

                    Android 11+
                

                

                    Pair device using Android native Wireless Debugging dialog in Developer Options.
                

                

                    Tip: Open Developer Options in Split Screen or Pop-up Window so Android does not rotate the 6-digit pairing code before you submit it. Every address field accepts a full IP:port (e.g. 192.168.1.20:37099) or just the port.
                

                

                    
                    
                


                
                
STEP 1: PAIR WITH CODE

                
Pairing address (IP:port or port)

                

                    
                    
                

                

                    
                    
                

                

                    Pair via Notification drops a notification with a reply box, so you can type the 6-digit code straight from the shade while Android's pairing dialog is on screen — no need to switch back to this app.
                


                
                
STEP 2: CONNECT WIRELESS ADB

                
Connect address from Wireless Debugging (IP:port or port)

                

                    
                    
                

                

                    
                    
                    
                

            


            
            

                

                    

                        Shizuku ADB Service
                    

                    Checking...
                

                

                    Uses the system Shizuku service to execute commands under shell UID 2000 without root. Works alongside ADB TCP 5555 — authorizing Shizuku switches to it.
                

                

                    
                    
                    
                

            


            
            

                

                    

                        Root (Superuser - su)
                    

                    Checking...
                

                

                    Full unrestricted root access on rooted Samsung / Magisk / KernelSU / APatch devices.
                

                

                    
                

            


            
            

                

                    

                        Read-Only Mode (Unprivileged)
                    

                    Safe
                

                

                    Allows inspecting all installed applications, package names, activities, and permissions safely without modifying packages.

Add a device

                        
Pair and connect over Wi-Fi, or link a watch over Bluetooth

                    

                

                
✕

            

            

                
                
                
            


            

                
On the device open Developer options and turn on Wireless debugging (on a Wear OS watch: ADB debugging, then Debug over Wi-Fi). Both must be on the same Wi-Fi network.

                
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
            


            

                
Looks on this Wi-Fi network for devices that offer wireless debugging. A device that waits for a pairing code shows up with Pair, one that is already paired shows up with Connect.

                
                

            


            

                
A Wear OS watch can be reached over its Bluetooth link to the phone, with no Wi-Fi. This phone then talks to the watch through its own ADB.

                
    
                    
  1. On the watch: Settings, Developer options, ADB debugging on, then Debug over Bluetooth on.
    2. 
                    
  2. In the Wear OS app on this phone: Watch settings, Advanced, Debugging over Bluetooth on.
    3. 
                    
  3. Turn on ADB in this app's Working mode, so this phone can reach itself.
    4. 
                    
  4. Tap the button below, then allow the connection on the watch.
    5.
